Turbulence

TUR-byuh-lens — think of a sputtering 'turbo' engine; turbulence is the rough, unsteady shaking of the ride. · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Turbulence is violent or unsteady movement, especially in air or water.

The captain warned passengers to fasten their seatbelts before flying through an area of expected turbulence.

Worked Example

A small boat crossing a calm lake suddenly hits a stretch of churning rapids, tossing and rocking violently from side to side as the crew scrambles to hold on.

That violent, unsteady, unpredictable motion in the water is exactly what turbulence means. Unlike 'current,' which just describes a steady flow, turbulence means rough, disordered movement.

How Turbulence Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

unrest

unrest: a state of disturbance or disorder

turmoil

turmoil: a state of great disturbance or confusion

upheaval

upheaval: a violent or sudden disruption

Antonyms

calm

calm: a state of stillness or peace

stability

stability: the state of being steady and unchanging

How Strong Is It? — unrest → turbulence → upheaval

unrest vs. turbulence

unrest vs. turbulence: Unrest is weaker than turbulence in a physical sense — unrest often describes ongoing tension, while turbulence describes violent, immediate, physical shaking.

upheaval vs. turbulence

upheaval vs. turbulence: Upheaval can be stronger than turbulence: turbulence describes rough, unsteady movement, but upheaval suggests something is being completely overturned or thrown into chaos.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — turb-

root — turb-: to disturb, throw into disorder (Latin (turbare))

suffix — -ulence

suffix — -ulence: full of, state of (Latin)

Put it together

Put it together: Latin turbare meant 'to disturb, throw into confusion,' related to turba, 'crowd, disorder.' Turbulence is, at its root, a state completely full of disturbance and disorder.

Use the root in a new word: disturb

Use the root in a new word: disturb: Please don't disturb the sleeping baby.
